column2: Jazz emerged from African-American musical communities in New Orleans around the turn of the 20th century.
Ragtime, blues, spirituals, marches and dance music all contributed to early jazz.
Early New Orleans ensembles often improvised several independent melodies together.
Arranged swing big bands became prominent dance music during the 1930s.
Bebop developed in the 1940s, favoring small ensembles and challenging, fast improvisation.
Cool jazz explored restrained textures and longer melodic lines from the late 1940s.
Hard bop emerged in the 1950s and drew on gospel, blues and rhythm-and-blues.
Modal jazz builds improvisation around modes, rather than only chord sequences.
Free jazz questioned fixed chord progressions, meter and conventional ensemble roles.
Jazz fusion combined jazz improvisation with rock rhythms and electric instruments in the late 1960s.
A jazz standard is a composition repeatedly reinterpreted by jazz performers.
Jazz evolved differently across countries as musicians adopted local musical traditions.
Chicago was a key center for hot jazz during the 1920s Jazz Age.
Louis Armstrong joined Fletcher Henderson's orchestra as a featured soloist in 1924.
Kid Ory's group recorded in Los Angeles during 1922.
Jazz improvisation often transforms a familiar melody through new phrasing, rhythm, harmony, or timbre.
A chorus is one complete pass through a tune's form; soloists may improvise several choruses.
A twelve-bar blues usually repeats a harmonic cycle of twelve measures, not necessarily twelve beats.
The common AABA song form has four eight-bar sections, but jazz arrangements may vary their length.
A head is the melody played near the start and end of many small-group jazz performances.
A turnaround is a short harmonic passage that leads from the end of a form back to its beginning.
A ii-V-I progression links predominant, dominant, and tonic harmony; it appears throughout jazz standards.
A tritone substitution replaces a dominant seventh chord with one whose root is a tritone away.
Chord extensions such as ninths, elevenths, and thirteenths enrich jazz voicings.
A shell voicing may use only a chord's root, third, and seventh, leaving room for the ensemble.
The third and seventh of a seventh chord often guide the listener through a jazz progression.
A lead sheet gives melody and chord symbols rather than a full arrangement.
A fake book compiles lead sheets so musicians can perform songs without full scores.
A jazz standard stays in circulation because generations of musicians keep reinterpreting it.
A contrafact is a new melody composed over the chord changes of an existing tune.
Rhythm changes refer to the harmonic pattern associated with Gershwin's I Got Rhythm.
Modal jazz allows long improvisations over one or a few modes instead of frequent chord changes.
A pedal point holds or repeats one bass pitch while harmony moves above it.
A blue note bends or colors a scale degree in a way that resists simple equal-tempered notation.
Call and response can pass a musical idea between soloist and ensemble, or between two instruments.
Swing feel often places successive eighth notes unevenly; no single ratio defines every swing tempo.
At faster tempos, swung eighth notes often become closer to equal length.
Syncopation stresses unexpected beats or subdivisions, creating tension against the underlying pulse.
A walking bass usually places a note on each quarter-note beat to connect harmony and time.
Comping is the pianist's or guitarist's rhythmic and harmonic support behind a soloist.
A drummer's ride cymbal can outline the main swing pulse while snare and bass drum add accents.
Brushes let drummers create a soft continuous texture as well as sharply articulated accents.
A break briefly leaves space for one player while the rest of the band stops.
Trading fours means musicians alternate four-measure solos, often with a drummer.
A stop-time passage punctuates occasional ensemble hits while a soloist fills the gaps.
A shuffle rhythm divides beats into a recurring long-short pattern associated with blues and swing.
Jazz can be played in straight eighths, swing eighths, or changing mixtures of both.
Odd meters such as 5/4 and 7/4 became distinctive colors in some modern jazz compositions.
Polyrhythm layers contrasting rhythmic groupings over a shared span of time.
Metric displacement makes a familiar phrase sound as though it starts on a different beat.
Behind-the-beat phrasing can sound relaxed while remaining connected to a steady rhythm section.
A vamp repeats a short harmonic or rhythmic figure beneath a solo or transition.
An ostinato is a repeating musical pattern; in jazz it can anchor a groove or modal passage.
A bass ostinato and walking bass produce different sensations even over the same harmony.
Silence can be an improvisational choice: a well-placed rest changes how the next phrase is heard.
The cornet and trumpet share much of their range, but players often describe different tone colors.
A plunger mute changes a brass instrument's resonance to create speechlike effects.
A growl on trumpet or trombone can combine altered embouchure with mute or vocal effects.
Saxophones transpose: an alto is normally in E-flat and a tenor normally in B-flat.
The saxophone is a woodwind instrument even though its body is normally made of metal.
A clarinet overblows at the twelfth, a feature that affects its fingering and wide register.
A double bass can provide pitched timekeeping without playing chords.
Pizzicato, or plucked bass, became central to the walking-bass sound.
Stride piano alternates low bass notes and midrange chords under a lively right hand.
The Hammond organ can sustain chords while a player shapes tone with drawbars and expression pedal.
The electric piano introduced a different attack and sustain to many jazz-fusion recordings.
Guitarists can create chord melodies that combine a tune's melody and accompaniment.
Scat singing improvises melodic lines with syllables rather than conventional lyrics.
Vocalese sets words to a pre-existing instrumental jazz solo; it differs from scat.
The human voice can bend blue notes and vary its attack much like an instrumental solo.
New Orleans jazz often used collective improvisation with several melodic lines at once.
Second-line parade traditions contributed rhythmic and social practices to New Orleans music.
Early jazz blended blues, brass-band practices, ragtime, and dance music.
Ragtime's syncopated piano writing preceded many early jazz recordings.
The Original Dixieland Jass Band made widely distributed jazz recordings in 1917.
King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band recorded with Louis Armstrong in 1923.
Louis Armstrong helped establish the improvising soloist as a central jazz figure.
Duke Ellington wrote arrangements with the individual sounds of his band members in mind.
Ellington's orchestra remained a creative laboratory for compositions across many decades.
The Cotton Club helped popularize Harlem big-band jazz while enforcing discriminatory admission practices.
Kansas City jazz emphasized blues riffs, extended improvisation, and a propulsive beat.
Count Basie's rhythm section became famous for a light but powerful swing feel.
The swing era made jazz central to American popular dance music in the 1930s.
Big bands commonly separated trumpets, trombones, and reeds into arranging sections.
Riff-based arranging builds music from short repeated phrases traded across sections.
Bebop grew in 1940s jam sessions and foregrounded complex, fast melodic improvisation.
Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie were pivotal voices in early bebop.
Bebop drumming often shifted accents away from a steady four-on-the-floor bass drum.
Thelonious Monk used unusual intervals, silences, and distinctive harmonic turns.
Bud Powell's piano style helped translate bebop's single-note horn lines to keyboard.
Cool jazz explored softer dynamics and careful textures without abandoning improvisation.
West Coast jazz became associated with several cool-jazz ensembles, but the styles are not identical.
Hard bop mixed bebop language with stronger blues and gospel influences.
Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers became a major training ground for generations of players.
Horace Silver combined hard-bop arrangements with blues and gospel-rooted phrases.
Miles Davis's Kind of Blue is closely associated with modal jazz.
John Coltrane explored intricate harmonic cycles before pursuing longer modal and free approaches.
Giant Steps is famous for its rapid shifts among distant key centers.
The Bill Evans Trio helped bring highly interactive bass-and-drum conversation into piano-trio jazz.
Ornette Coleman's work challenged fixed chord progressions and traditional solo structures.
Free jazz does not necessarily mean random playing: musicians may organize around motives and collective listening.
Sun Ra combined adventurous big-band writing with futuristic imagery and theater.
Charles Mingus combined compositional detail with intense ensemble improvisation.
Eric Dolphy expanded jazz timbres with bass clarinet and other woodwinds.
Jazz fusion brought rock grooves and electric instruments into new improvising ensembles.
Herbie Hancock's Headhunters period blended jazz harmony with funk-driven rhythms.
Weather Report explored large-scale textures with electric keyboards and bass.
Bossa nova blends Brazilian samba influences with understated singing and sophisticated harmony.
Joao Gilberto's guitar rhythm and soft vocal phrasing became hallmarks of bossa nova.
Afro-Cuban jazz joins jazz improvisation with clave-based rhythmic traditions.
Clave is a structural rhythmic pattern, not merely a percussion instrument.
Latin jazz includes distinct Afro-Cuban and Brazilian traditions rather than one uniform beat.
Third stream sought ways to combine jazz methods with classical composition.
European jazz scenes developed distinctive improvising traditions rather than only copying US styles.
Gypsy jazz is associated with the guitar virtuosity and ensemble style of Django Reinhardt.
Jazz manouche ensembles often feature acoustic guitars and violin instead of a conventional drum kit.
The Newport Jazz Festival began in 1954 and helped establish the outdoor jazz-festival model.
The Village Vanguard is a New York club associated with landmark live jazz recordings.
A jam session lets musicians improvise together outside a fully rehearsed concert format.
Live recordings preserve audience energy, room acoustics, and musical decisions that studio edits may hide.
Mono recordings combine channels into one, yet early jazz performances can remain rhythmically vivid.
A chorus count tells you the form cycles a soloist takes; it is not a measure of how loud they play.
To follow a solo, try humming the tune's opening phrase while the improvisation unfolds.
Listening to the bass often reveals where a jazz band is in the harmonic cycle.
A drummer may imply the pulse on cymbals while playing sparse, surprising snare accents.
A repeated two-bar phrase can become more exciting through changing accents than through added notes.
Compare two recordings of the same standard to hear how tempo and voicing alter its character.
Recognizing a familiar tune beneath a contrafact reveals how bebop players reworked existing harmony.
A ballad tempo leaves more space between phrases, making tone and breath especially expressive.
Improvising slowly can expose voice-leading choices that flash by during fast solos.
Learning a solo by ear develops phrasing and articulation as well as note recognition.
A metronome on beats two and four is a common practice exercise for internalizing swing time.
A guide-tone line built from thirds and sevenths can outline chord changes without a full accompaniment.
Playing a standard in multiple keys builds flexibility for accompanying singers and other instruments.
Transposition lets a horn player read a written pitch different from the sounding concert pitch.
A guitarist may leave out the root when the bassist already makes it clear.
A small ensemble can sound fuller through contrasting register and rhythm rather than constant chords.
In a jazz combo, good accompaniment responds to the soloist instead of repeating a rigid pattern.
Improvisers sometimes quote another tune as a playful commentary inside a solo.
Different takes of a standard can expose spontaneous decisions even with the same musicians.
The same walking line may outline several chord substitutions, so listen for piano and horn clues too.
Jazz notation may specify chord symbols while leaving articulation and timing to performers.
A good jazz arrangement can alternate written ensemble passages with completely improvised solos.
The groove in a jazz performance depends on how musicians coordinate their timing, not just its BPM.
A strong melodic motif can bind a long solo together even while the underlying harmony changes.
Tension and release in jazz may come from rhythm, register, dynamics, and silence as much as harmony.
Blue notes are expressive inflections; they need not fit one fixed pitch frequency in every performance.
The term 'jazz' covers many approaches, and not every jazz performance uses a swung rhythm.
The rhythm section traditionally supports time and harmony, but modern jazz often makes it equally conversational.
Collective improvisation means several players create compatible lines at the same time.
All musicians are subconsciously mathematicians.
My band is my instrument more than the piano.
The piano ain't got no wrong notes.
My ego only needs a good rhythm section.
So go on and play, and if you make a mistake, make it loud so you won't make it next time.
If you still have to ask, shame on you
Playing "Bop" is like playing Scrabble with all the vowels missing.
In my music, I'm trying to play the truth of what I am.
I always wanted to be a spontaneous composer.
As the painter needs his framework of parchment, the improvising musical group needs its framework in time.
Jazz is about being in the moment, at every moment.
Jazz is about trusting yourself to respond on the fly.
To be a musician is really something. It goes very, very deep.
My music is the spiritual expression of what I am
I'm always making a comeback but nobody ever tells me where I've been.
Let's play the music and not the background!
I wanted to be heard. That's why I'm broke.
Play like you play. Play like you think, and then you got it, if you're going to get it.
I write music to celebrate life.
It's the joy of creating. It's a way of life.
I think that virtuosity is the first sign of morality in a musician.
Calling me a jazz singer was a way of ignoring my musical background
The only thing I'm interested in is the music and the musicians.
jazz should have the right to take big chances
the whole idea of jazz is that if you think of a phrase, you should be able to play it
